# Simulation Design and Performance Evaluation

In this section, we present the simulation design and performance metrics for the two simulation studies. The information presented here follows the suggestions from previous articles that investigated the quality of simulation studies [@siepe_etall_2024; @white_etall_2024; @morris_etall_2019].

## Simulation Conditions

Both simulations used a 2 (sample sizes) × 3 (reliability levels) × 3 (latent predictor distributions) factorial design, yielding 18 conditions. Simulation 1 evaluated UPI, LMS, QML, and LSAM; Simulation 2 excluded LMS due to computational constraints. To assess Type I error rates and empirical local power [@irmer_etall_2024], we tested two specifications: (a) linear model data generation with full model estimation (assessing Type I error), and (b) full interaction model for both generation and estimation (assessing power). This yielded 36 total conditions, each replicated 1,000 times.

Sample sizes of 400 and 1000 represented moderate to large samples. We selected 400 to examine performance below the suggested 500-threshold minimum for complex latent interaction models (Wall et al., 2012) while remaining realistic for applied research. The 1000 sample size allowed evaluation of asymptotic properties and aligned with previous simulations. Three reliability levels (0.4, 0.6, 0.8—termed low, medium, and high) covered a broad range of measurement quality. While previous simulations typically examined high reliability [@brandt_etall_2014; @lonati_etall_2024] or contrasted high versus low [e.g., 0.8 and 0.5 in Brandt_etall_2020], we included 0.4 to assess performance under poor measurement conditions. Last, the three distributional conditions—normal, non-normal, and uniform—were based on prior research varying non-normality to different degrees [@brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @cham_etall_2012; @lonati_etall_2024; @wall_amemiya_2000]. We used a copula-based approach termed Vine-To-Anything (VITA) to circumvent the issues associated with other data generation pproaches used in previous simulation studies [@gronneberg_foldnes_2022].

## Data Generation

Data generation followed a similar procedure as in previous studies [@ng_chan_2020; @cox_kelcey_2021; @rosseel_etall_2025]. First, structural residual variances and measurement error variances were set to achieve $R^2 \approx 0.30$ and reliability $\rho \in \{0.4, 0.6, 0.8\}$ under normally distributed predictor latent variables. Second, using these fixed variance parameters, data were generated under three distributional conditions (see Appendix A for complete data generation procedures). See Figure 1 for the true population models. 

For Simulation 1, the dependent latent variable was generated according to:
\begin{align*}
\eta_3 = \beta_{30} + \beta_{31}\eta_1 + \beta_{32}\eta_2 + \beta_{33}(\eta_1\eta_2) + \beta_{34}\eta_1^2 + \beta_{35}\eta_2^2 + \zeta
\end{align*}
\noindent with parameters $\beta_{30} = -0.255$, $\beta_{31} = \beta_{32} = 0.316$, $\beta_{33} = 0.139$, $\beta_{34} = \beta_{35} = 0.101$, and $\zeta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{33})$. For the linear model comparison, nonlinear terms were omitted ($\beta_{33} = \beta_{34} = \beta_{35} = 0$).

For Simulation 2, similarly as above, the dependent latent variables was generated as follows:
\begin{align*}
\eta_4 &= \beta_{40} + \beta_{41}\eta_1 + \beta_{42}\eta_2 + \beta_{43}\eta_3 + \beta_{44}(\eta_1\eta_2) + \beta_{45}(\eta_1\eta_3) + \beta_{46}\eta_1^2 + \beta_{47}\eta_2^2 + \zeta_4 \\
\eta_5 &= \beta_{50} + \beta_{51}\eta_4 + \beta_{52}\eta_1 + \beta_{53}\eta_2 + \beta_{54}\eta_3 + \beta_{55}(\eta_1\eta_4) + \beta_{56}(\eta_2\eta_4) + \beta_{57}\eta_1^2 + \beta_{58}\eta_3^2 + \zeta_5
\end{align*}

\noindent with parameters $\beta_{40} = \beta_{50} = 0.1$, $\beta_{41} = \beta_{42} = \beta_{43} = 0.20$, $\beta_{44} = \beta_{45} = 0.11$, $\beta_{46} = \beta_{47} = 0.08$; $\beta_{51} = \beta_{52} = \beta_{53} = \beta_{54} = 0.16$, $\beta_{55} = \beta_{56} = 0.08$, $\beta_{57} = \beta_{58} = 0.06$, and $\zeta_4 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{44})$, $\zeta_5 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{55})$. For the linear model comparison, all interaction and quadratic terms were omitted.

## Reproducibility and Computational Details^[All the materials to reproduce this article available on the following GitHub link: https://github.com/felipelfv/Simulation_First_PhD_Article.git. We included a `README` file that contains the step-by-step information required to reproduce the results reported, a `sessionInfo` file, the *renv* lockfile with the information for the remaining relevant packages used [@R-renv], a Dockerfile for system dependencies, and all the estimates obtained for all iterations. Moreover, this paper was written with *papaja* [@R-papaja] in Rmarkdown.]

The simulation was conducted on a Mac Studio with an Apple M4 Max chip (with 14 cores and 36 GB of RAM), running macOS Sequoia 15.5. All analyses were performed in R [@R-base] (version `r R_version`). Parallel processing was implemented through the *doParalell* package (version `r doparallel_version`) [@R-doParallel], with *doRNG* (version `r dorng_version`) [@R-doRNG] to ensure independent and reproducible random number streams. For the UPI, LMS, and QML approach, the *modsem* package was used [@kjell_etall_2024] (version `r modsem_version`). For the LSAM approach, the *lavaan* package was used [@R-lavaan] (version `r lavaan_version`). Importantly, we used the default settings for the functions provided in the packages^[This is important to acknowledge because there are arguments for the functions used that, in principle, could be tweaked to obtain better results. For instance, one could change the maximum steps for the M-step in the EM algorithm for the LMS. However, this also leads to substantial researcher degrees of freedom and hence were avoided.]. One important exception is that for the LSAM we estimated the latent factors with a single measurement block as opposed to separately to maintain some similarity with the other approaches [@rosseel_loh_2024]. Finally, for generating normal, non-normal, and uniform data we used the *covsim*  (version `r covsim_version`) [@R-covsim] and *rvinecopulib* (version `r vinecop`) [@].

## Nonconvergence and Outliers

Before analyzing the data, we identified non-convergent solutions as those where estimates for the parameters of interest were not produced. Following @lonati_etall_2024, we excluded the entire iteration from the analysis across estimation approaches as non-convergent solutions signal replications challenging for all methods^[Convergent solutions may still be implausible or incomplete. For instance, where estimates for other parameters in the model are not obtained. Thus, we tracked these via warnings and obtained qualitatively identical results if excluding from the analysis (results available on GitHub).]. We calculated convergence rate as $\text{Convergence}_{rate} = N_{\text{complete}}/N_{\text{total}} \times 100\%$, where $N_{\text{complete}}$ represents successfully converged replications with complete output for that specific approach and $N_{\text{total}}$ represents all attempted replications for the same approach.

Similar to @lonati_etall_2024 as well, we identified outliers using the box-plot method applied to iterations where all methods successfully converged. For each method-parameter combination, quartiles and interquartile ranges were calculated from this common set of converged iterations, and estimates outside $[Q_1 - 3 \times \text{IQR}, Q_3 + 3 \times \text{IQR}]$ (where $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$) were flagged as outliers. Following the same exclusion logic as for convergence failures, we excluded the entire iteration from the analysis across all estimation approaches when any method produced an outlier point estimate for any parameter. To avoid possible arbitrary threshold selection, we also computed median-based metrics before outlier removal.

## Performance Measures

Method performance was assessed through multiple metrics following the formulas from the *simhelpers* package [@R-simhelpers], with the exception of the median-based metrics that were based on @brandt_etall_2020. Following the *simhelpers* documentation and references therein, we also quantified the Monte Carlo Standard Errors (MCSE) simulation uncertainty for most of the reported performance measures using the jack-knife technique. Generally speaking, the measures are classified in terms of absolute and relative criteria measures, standard error assessment, hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals. In the main text, we only report and discuss the metrics reported in Table 1 for the interaction and quadratic effects. For the complete set of measures and main effects, we refer the reader to the online supplementary materials 1.
